turns.name: write_review
turns.finalText:
BRAF-targeted therapies have revolutionized the treatment of advanced melanoma, significantly improving outcomes for the more than 50% of patients whose tumors harbor BRAF mutations that aberrantly activate the MAPK/ERK pathway [1, 2, 3]. While these targeted treatments provide marked clinical benefits, their long-term efficacy is frequently compromised by the emergence of acquired therapeutic resistance, which remains the central barrier to durable disease control [4, 5]. 

Melanoma cells evade BRAF inhibition through several distinct resistance mechanisms. These include compensatory activation of the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway [4], epigenetic dysregulation driven by the histone methyltransferases G9a and EZH2 [6], and a phenotypic switch from an epithelial to a more aggressive mesenchymal state characterized by high AXL expression [7]. To overcome these barriers, emerging combination strategies are being actively developed. Current approaches emphasize integrating BRAF-targeted therapies with immune checkpoint inhibitors [1, 2, 5], as well as utilizing novel targeted agents like AXL inhibitors [7] or compounds such as diosmetin to concurrently suppress both the MAPK and STAT3 pathways [4].

**Evidence boundary:** The provided evidence establishes the high prevalence of BRAF mutations in melanoma, the clinical utility of BRAF inhibitors, specific molecular resistance mechanisms (JAK2/STAT3, AXL, G9a/EZH2), and the need for combination therapies (immunotherapy, AXL inhibitors). It does not detail specific overall survival statistics for these novel combinations or address resistance mechanisms exclusive to non-melanoma cancers beyond the provided colorectal cancer context.
